newsitem.title: USA: Ex-President Bush sees U.S.-China relations key.
newsitem.headline: Ex-President Bush sees U.S.-China relations key.

text.p: Former U.S. President George Bush, outlining what he saw as the key foreign U.S. foreign policy challenges that lie ahead, said Monday good relations with China should be a top priority.
In a keynote address to petroleum refiners assembled here, Bush said peace for the entire world was linked to solid U.S.-China relations.

"I believe that the U.S.-China relationship is the single most important bilateral relationship that this country has," Bush told executives attending the National Petroleum Refiners Association's annual meeting.

"I think that relationship has more to do with peace in the next millennium than any other relationship," he continued, adding that engaging China should not, however, come at the expense of other foreign policy concerns such as relations with Europe or democratization and privatization in Latin America.
Bush, who said he has been to China eight times since losing his 1992 re-election bid to Bill Clinton, said he was concerned there was little understanding in Congress of China.
He added he was happy the top three U.S. leaders, Clinton, Vice President Al Gore and Newt Gingrich, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, all had China trips on their agendas.
"Whoever is in the leadership, regardless of party, needs to understand China. It is very very essential that we not neglect China," Bush said.
In the 30-minute address, he also critiqued current thinking on China in both political parties.
He said Republican calls for "containment" were made without knowledge of what "Chinese leaders want."
He added, "We shouldn't build a foreign policy on containment. We ought to build it on consultation and dialogue."

He also said "left-wing" Democrats trying to lecture and humiliate China over human rights was the wrong approach. "This public lecturing that everybody should be just like us is not the way you deal, not just with China, but with other countries in Asia as well."
Bush said human rights in China were now, in his view, undoubtedly better than when he served as the equivalent of U.S. ambassador to China from 1974 to 1975.

He recalled that in 1989 as President, he balanced the human rights versus engagement issues by imposing sanctions on China after pro-democracy demonstrators were massacred in Beijing's Tiannanmen Square all while preserving most favored nation trading status for China.
He also said he was puzzled about recent allegations that China may have tried to buy influence in the 1996 U.S. Presidential election, noting he thought the matter should be "fully investigated."

Bush said, "In terms of this scandal that's bustling around, I know nothing about it, but I would simply say get the facts. Bring to justice those who accepted tainted money. And then get on with the essential foreign policy goal of improving our relationship with the countries of Asia."
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk 212-859-1620
